summary: Specifies the cryptographic algorithms and attributes that TCP-AO can use with its manual keying mechanism, and defines how new message authentication codes can be added. Both ends must use the same algorithms to interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Two people using a secret code must pick the same code book. This lists the code books TCP-AO can use.

questions: why is the tcp-ao mac truncated to 96 bits
subtitle: The two MAC algorithms and two key derivation functions every TCP-AO implementation must support.

tldr.problem: TCP-AO lets users pick their cryptographic algorithms, so implementations need a common mandatory set to interoperate and a way to add more later.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5926 requires two MACs (HMAC-SHA-1-96 and AES-128-CMAC-96) and two matching key derivation functions (KDF_HMAC_SHA1 and KDF_AES_128_CMAC), which turn a shared Master_Key into per-connection Traffic_Keys. MAC outputs are cut to 96 bits to fit the option field.
tldr.outcome: All four components must be implemented for full compliance. The RFC also sets requirements for future algorithms and creates an IANA registry for them.

today: RFC 5926 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the cryptography used with the TCP Authentication Option in RFC 5925.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document is a companion to RFC 5925, the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO). TCP-AO provides cryptographic authentication and message integrity verification between two end-points, using message authentication codes (MACs) that rely on shared keys. Hash-based MACs (HMACs) are defined in RFC 2104, and cipher-based MACs (CMACs) in NIST SP 800-38B.

RFC 5926 defines the general requirements for MACs used in TCP-AO, for current and future algorithms. It specifies two MAC algorithms and two key derivation functions (KDFs) that all TCP-AO implementations are required to have.
sections.eli5: TCP-AO is a way to sign each message. This document says which signing methods everyone must know.

sections.title: Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
This is the initial specification of required cryptography for TCP-AO. All four components MUST be implemented for an implementation to be fully compliant: HMAC-SHA-1-96 and AES-128-CMAC-96 as authentication algorithms, and KDF_HMAC_SHA1 and KDF_AES_128_CMAC as key derivation functions.

TCP-AO is meant to support cryptographic agility. For future MAC algorithms, the RFC says they SHOULD protect at least 2 to the power of 48 messages with a collision probability of less than one in 10 to the power of 9.
sections.eli5: Everyone must carry two stamps and two ways to make ink. New stamps can be added later if they are strong enough.

sections.title: Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
TCP-AO uses a KDF to turn a Master_Key into a Traffic_Key, the key that authenticates the segments of one connection. The interface is Traffic_Key = KDF_alg(Master_Key, Context, Output_Length). In manual keying the Master_Key is a pre-shared key of variable length. The management interface MUST accept ASCII strings and SHOULD also allow arbitrary binary strings in hexadecimal. The Context comes from RFC 5925, and Output_Length is the key size, in bits, that the MAC needs.

Both KDFs use the counter mode of NIST SP 800-108. Each block fed to the pseudorandom function is ( i || Label || Context || Output_Length ). The counter i is one octet starting at 1, the Label is the ASCII string TCP-AO, and Output_Length takes two octets. Outputs of repeated calls are concatenated and the last one truncated as needed.

KDF_HMAC_SHA1 uses HMAC-SHA1 and produces 160 bits. KDF_AES_128_CMAC uses AES-CMAC and produces 128 bits. Because AES-CMAC needs a key of exactly 16 octets, a Master_Key of any other length is first run through AES-CMAC with an all-zero 128-bit key, as in RFC 4615, to give the key K. A 16-octet Master_Key is used as is. The RFC recommends a randomly generated 128-bit Master_Key.

For user interfaces, KDF_HMAC_SHA1 SHOULD be shown as "SHA1", KDF_AES_128_CMAC as "AES128", and KDF_HMAC_SHA1 SHOULD be the default because it is widely supported.
sections.eli5: From one shared secret, each connection gets its own special key, made by mixing in details of that connection. A short or long secret is first reshaped to the right size.

sections.title: The MAC Algorithms
sections.content:
Each MAC algorithm defined for TCP-AO has three fixed elements: the KDF_Alg that makes its Traffic_Key, the Key_Length in bits, and the MAC_Length, the bits that end up in the TCP-AO MAC field. The interface is MAC = MAC_alg(Traffic_Key, Message), where the message is defined in RFC 5925. Each MAC algorithm MUST name its KDF, though a KDF MAY serve several MACs.

The two algorithms are HMAC-SHA-1-96 (KDF_HMAC_SHA1, key length 160 bits, MAC length 96 bits) and AES-128-CMAC-96 (KDF_AES_128_CMAC, key length 128 bits, MAC length 96 bits). The full outputs are 160 bits for HMAC-SHA-1 and 128 bits for AES-128-CMAC, and both are truncated to 96 bits as a trade-off between security and message size so they fit the option field.

The RFC says AES-128-CMAC-96 is potentially more efficient, particularly in hardware, while HMAC-SHA-1-96 is more widely used and usually needs little or no new code.
sections.eli5: Both methods make a short fingerprint of each message, then keep only the first part of it so it fits in the small space available.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document inherits the security considerations of TCP-AO, AES-CMAC and HMAC-SHA-1. Security depends on both the algorithms and on keys that are unpredictable, and RFC 4086 is pointed to for key generation. Accepting short Master_Keys is a convenience and does not mean weak keys are safe.

Two MACs are mandated after discussion in the TCPM working group and with the Security Area Directors. SHA-1 is a MUST because it is widely deployed with enough strength and reasonable cost, and the 96-bit truncation helps. AES-128 CMAC is considered stronger but less widely implemented, and is a MUST to drive vendors toward it and give another option if SHA-1 were compromised.

The RFC expects that some algorithms may later prove weaker than believed and that new revisions will be issued, and tells implementers to look for more recent versions.
sections.eli5: Keep your secret hard to guess. Having two methods means there is a spare if one turns out to be weak.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content: IANA created a registry named "Cryptographic Algorithms for TCP-AO", with the registration procedure "RFC Publication after Expert Review". Its initial contents are two entries, SHA1 and AES128, both referencing RFC 5926.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of approved methods, and it starts with two.
